bib.title: Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs

read.skipped: References skimmed only. Figure data (Figs 1-8) is number soup in the text; table values were taken from tables, figure values noted as read from the figure text.

question: Do o1-like reasoning models spend test-time compute efficiently, and can self-training reduce wasted tokens on simple problems without losing accuracy?
hypothesis: Later solutions in o1-like responses add little accuracy or diversity, so training the model on streamlined self-generated responses should cut tokens while keeping accuracy.
contributions: First study offering an explanation and analysis of overthinking: o1-like LLMs often expend unnecessary compute on redundant solutions that contribute minimally to final outcomes.
Outcome and process efficiency metrics for o1-like models.
Self-training strategies to mitigate overthinking that cut tokens while keeping performance across testsets of varying difficulty.

method.summary: Analyse solution counts, first-correct position and strategy diversity of QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1 outputs on ASDIV, GSM8K and MATH500, define two token-efficiency metrics, then fine-tune QwQ-32B-Preview on its own shortened responses (SFT, DPO, RPO, SimPO) built from PRM12K samples.
method.task: Math reasoning (efficiency of long chain-of-thought) and length-preference post-training

datasets.name: MATH500
datasets.size: 500 problems (name only; count not stated in text)

datasets.name: PRM12K
datasets.preprocessing: Samples without a correct answer discarded; solutions separated from responses with Llama-3.3-70B; shortest result of each simplification type chosen from 10 samples.

other.note: Base for post-training; chosen because it is available for post-training.

other.also: used to separate solutions from responses

other.use: cluster solutions by reasoning strategy for the distinctness ratio

training.objective: SFT (cross-entropy on shortest correct response); DPO; RPO (DPO plus NLL term on preferred response); SimPO (reference-free, adaptive margin and length regularisation). Preference pairs: positive = shortest or simplified response, negative = longest of 10 samples (greedy-search negative was less effective in preliminary experiments).

other.positive_example_types: Shortest Response; First-Correct Solutions (FCS); FCS+Reflection (adds second correct solution); Greedily Diverse Solutions (GDS)

inference.decoding: Greedy search for the evaluations of Tables 1 and 4 (inferred: Table 2 labels a Greedy response type; evaluation decoding is not stated)
inference.temperature: 1.0 for sampling 10 training responses per instance
inference.samples: 10 samples per training instance; evaluation run count not stated

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.definition: Correct answers (for o1-like models, sigma_i = 1 if at least one solution in the response is correct is used in the outcome metric)

metrics.name: #Solution
metrics.definition: Number of solution rounds in a response, where a solution is part of the generation that explicitly contains an answer

metrics.name: Outcome efficiency xi_O
metrics.definition: (1/N) sum_i sigma_i * T_hat_i / T_i; T_hat_i = tokens to first correct answer if sigma_i=1, else T_i

metrics.name: Process efficiency xi_P
metrics.definition: (1/N) sum_i D_i / T_i; D_i = tokens in solutions that introduce a new reasoning strategy (GPT-4o clustering)

metrics.name: Distinctness ratio
metrics.definition: Share of m-th solutions whose strategy is not among those of solutions 1..m-1

eval.protocol: Single reported number per cell; no seeds, variance or significance tests stated.

prompts.purpose: GPT-4o clustering of solutions by reasoning strategy
prompts.text: Criteria for clustering the mathematical solutions: 1. If the solutions used to arrive at the solutions are fundamentally different from each other, such as algebraic manipulation versus geometric reasoning, they can be considered novel; 2. Even if the results are the same, if the intermediate steps or processes involved in reaching those solutions vary significantly, the solutions can be considered different; 3. If the solutions relies on different assumptions or conditions, they should be considered different from each other; 4. A solution might generalize to a broader class of problems, while another solution might be specific to certain conditions. In such cases, they are considered distinct; 5. If one solution is significantly simpler or more complex than the others, it can be regarded as essentially novel, even if they lead to the same result. Given the following mathematical problem: ***problem*** Solutions: Solution 1: ... Solution 2: ... Please output the clusters strictly following the following format, each row containing a cluster, names, and reasons. Do not include any additional text or explanations outside of this format: cluster1 [solution names] reason for cluster ...

evidence.quote: Hence, we adopt “FCS+Reflection” as the default response simplification method.
We generated 10 samples for each instance in the training dataset with a temperature of 1.0.

results.claim: On the trivial question 'what is the answer of 2 plus 3?', o1-like models use far more tokens than conventional models.
results.setup: Single question, Fig 1(a); o1-like models (QwQ-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1) vs conventional LLMs.
results.quote: On average, o1-like models consumed 1,953% more tokens than conventional models to reach the same answer.

results.claim: In over 92% of cases the first solution already gives the correct answer, so later solutions add little accuracy.
results.setup: QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1 on ASDIV and MATH500 (Fig 5: 93%, 90%, 89%, 97%).
results.quote: In more than 92% of cases, the initial round of solutions produces the correct answer.

results.claim: QwQ-32B-Preview first solution on ASDIV is a minority of the response tokens.
results.setup: QwQ-32B-Preview on ASDIV; first round averages 287 tokens.
results.quote: the average length of the first round of solutions for QwQ-32B-Preview on the ASDIV test set is 287 tokens, constituting only 38.7% of the entire response.

results.claim: o1-like models generate more solution rounds on easier problems: on MATH500 level 1-2 vs level 4-5, QwQ averages 3.7 vs 3.0 rounds.
results.setup: QwQ-32B-Preview (R1: 4.6 vs 3.9); token count still rises with difficulty.
results.quote: averaging 3.7 rounds and 4.6 rounds, respectively) compared to levels 4-5 (e.g., averaging 3.0 rounds and 3.9 rounds, respectively)

results.claim: Distinctness of later solutions falls: solution 2 often double-checks solution 1 with the same strategy.
results.metric: drop in distinctness ratio, solution >=4 vs solution 3
results.setup: Average across test sets, QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1 on ASDIV and MATH500; strategies clustered by GPT-4o.
results.quote: the average distinctness ratio for Solution#≥4 across test sets decreases by 11.5% compared to Solution#3

results.claim: Worked example: the 13-solution QwQ response to 2+3 has outcome efficiency 4.3%.
results.note: Text extraction splits the fraction over two lines; the process efficiency for the same example is 35.8%.

results.claim: o1-like models are far less efficient than conventional models on MATH500: QwQ-32B-Preview 93.0 accuracy with 2407.9 tokens and outcome efficiency 52.3%.
results.setup: MATH500; baseline is Qwen2.5-Math-72B-Instruct (1 solution, 593.1 tokens); DeepSeek-R1 96.4 accuracy, 2704.3 tokens, 51.0%.
results.table: Table 1, MATH500, row QwQ-32B-Preview, columns Accuracy 93.0, #Token 2407.9, Outcome 52.3%

results.claim: Overthinking is worst on easy problems: outcome efficiency under 50% at MATH500 level 1 for both models (QwQ 57.5% vs 46.4% from level 1 to level 5 readings are noisy in Fig 7).
results.quote: both models perform poorly on the simplest Level 1 problems, achieving less than 50% outcome efficiency
results.note: Fig 7 number soup lists values 57.5%, 54.7%, 49.8%, 46.8%, 46.4% and 74.5%... without clear axis labels, so which series is outcome vs process was not resolved from the text; the quote is the safe statement.

results.claim: The shortest of 10 sampled responses is more efficient than greedy (outcome 69.8% vs 55.6%), supporting self-improvement.
results.setup: QwQ-32B-Preview on PRM12K training data, 10 samples at temperature 1.0, correct only; shortest 2.5 solutions, 1051.3 tokens; greedy 3.1, 1434.8; longest 4.1, 2258.7 (46.0%).
results.table: Table 2, row Shortest, column Outcome 69.8%; row Greedy 55.6%

results.claim: FCS positives are the most efficient simplification (1.1 solutions, 681.0 tokens, outcome 99.5%, process 99.1%).
results.setup: Training data statistics; baseline is Shortest Response. FCS+Ref. 1.9 sol, 878.7 tokens, 78.4%/82.4%; GDS 1.6, 856.8, 86.8%/94.2%.

results.claim: SimPO with FCS+Reflection cuts tokens on MATH500 from 2407.9 to 1330.7 (about 48.6% fewer) at 92.8 vs 93.0 accuracy.
results.setup: QwQ-32B-Preview + SimPO with FCS+Reflection positives; outcome efficiency 52.3% to 80.0%, process 71.2% to 89.5%, solutions 3.2 to 1.9.
results.quote: our approach can reduce token output by 48.6% while maintaining accuracy on the widely-used MATH500 testset as applied to QwQ-32B-Preview.
results.note: Table 4 gives accuracy 92.8 vs 93.0; 'maintaining' is a 0.2-point drop on a single run.

results.claim: Among length-preference methods on MATH500 with Shortest Response positives, SimPO is best, reducing generated tokens by 22.3%; SFT barely changes length.
results.setup: MATH500, QwQ-32B-Preview. SFT 93.2 acc/2359.5 tokens; DPO 94.0/1929.5; RPO 91.6/2015.7; SimPO 92.4/1871.8.
results.quote: SimPO achieves the best results, reducing the number of generated tokens by 22.3% on MATH500.

results.claim: On easier sets the method keeps or raises accuracy with about half the tokens.
results.setup: SimPO FCS+Reflection; GSM8K 772.8 to 416.6 tokens, outcome 50.7% to 80.2%; ASDIV 96.9 to 96.8 accuracy, 741.8 to 381.6 tokens.
results.table: Table 4, GSM8K, row +SimPO FCS+Reflection, column Accuracy 96.0

results.claim: FCS alone loses accuracy on MATH500 (91.0 vs 93.0 vanilla) while using 1016.0 tokens; GDS gets 91.8.
results.setup: MATH500; FCS 1.4 solutions, outcome 88.7%, process 98.1%; GDS 1.7 solutions, 1286.1 tokens.
results.table: Table 4, MATH500, row +SimPO First-Correct Solution, column Accuracy 91.0

results.claim: On harder sets the method keeps accuracy with fewer tokens, with a small drop on AIME24 (43.3 vs 46.7) and GPQA (59.1 vs 59.6).
results.setup: QwQ-32B-Preview + SimPO FCS+Reflection; AIME24 tokens 9480.9 to 5154.5; GPQA tokens 3228.4 to 2085.7. AIME24 has 30 problems (inferred from 23.3/46.7/43.3 steps; not stated).
results.table: Table 4, AIME24, row +SimPO FCS+Reflection, column Accuracy 43.3
results.note: The paper reports this as maintaining performance; the AIME24 drop is 3.4 points.

limits: No limitations section. The conclusion lists future work: adaptive compute strategies that adjust to problem complexity, and refining efficiency metrics for broader model generalisation.

Training hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, epochs, SimPO beta and gamma, hardware), evaluation decoding, max tokens, and runs or seeds are not stated; no variance or significance tests, so differences of 0.2 to 3 points cannot be judged.
Efficiency metrics rely on Llama-3.3-70B splitting solutions and GPT-4o clustering strategies, with no validation of either step reported.
Post-training is done on only one model, QwQ-32B-Preview; DeepSeek-R1 is analysed but not trained.
Training data is PRM12K math only; claims are limited to math and GPQA.
The 'Efficiency' value on Fig 7 and the Fig 3-6 distributions come from figures whose text is unlabeled number soup.
Preliminary experiment that greedy-search negatives are less effective than longest-sample negatives is reported without numbers.
Dated: QwQ-32B-Preview and the o1-preview class of models; the paper describes DeepSeek-R1 results and cites the R1 paper from January 2025 (v2).
